t: Relevance and aim of the topic
n: This topic is devoted to determining the age of injuries and fractures. First, let us see why it is needed. In the clinic, the age of a fracture is needed for choosing the treatment, and for monitoring healing and adjusting therapy. In forensic medicine, bone injuries give information about the circumstances of an incident and, where necessary, help to determine the cause of death. When child abuse is suspected, the degree of healing helps establish the chronology of injuries and with whom the child was. The age of a wound also helps reconstruct the crime scene. With multiple injuries, their timing and sequence are established, because punishment differs according to severity.

t: Vitality and wound age: two main questions
n: Now the two main questions. The first: was the injury inflicted during life, in the agonal period or after death, and how long did the victim survive? The answer to this question is sought through vitality. Vitality means the reactions of the living organism to injury, that is, haemorrhage, infiltration by inflammatory cells and granulation tissue. The chain is as follows: injury inflicted, vital reactions appear, haemorrhage and inflammation, then granulation tissue, finally vitality and wound age. If vitality is confirmed, the post-traumatic interval, that is, PTI, substantiates the causal link between injury and death.

The topic relies on three sources. The first is Lawrence: the 2025 review, comparing 21 publications, evaluates imaging methods for determining fracture age. It studies the age of bone fractures, mainly on 2D radiographs. The second is Li: it considers wound age and vitality, covering skin, muscle and brain; articles in PubMed and the Chinese CNKI database were analysed. The third is Tomassini: it studies the age of skin injury with markers of immunohistochemistry, that is, IHC, and immunofluorescence, that is, IF. Thus bone, wounds in general and skin injury are covered in separate sources.

Determining the age of a fracture is difficult, for several reasons. First, healing has several biological signs, but the stages overlap, and each person passes through them at their own pace. Second, age and health status are believed to influence the rate of healing. But data for each group are scarce, and the effect is hard to measure. Third, in abuse, treatment may be delayed and the fracture site remains mobile. As a result, the bone may heal incorrectly or slowly. Remember: in a single fracture, several healing stages may be visible at the same time. Do not assume that one stage equals one exact time.

Now the search and selection stages of the review. Three conditions were set for the papers: the paper had to be peer-reviewed, in English and based on human data. The paper had to focus on methodology rather than be an individual case report, and the stages and their timing had to be clearly given. The search was carried out in summer 2024, and records up to July 2024 were reviewed. The screening chain is as follows: across 6 databases 1328 results, by title and abstract 259, after removing duplicates 86, by full text 10 suitable papers, and a further 11 were added from references, giving 21 publications in total.

Let us look at the demography of the literature. These 21 publications cover 1987–2024. In 1987–2010 only 4 papers appeared, and in 2011–2023 a further 16 were published. The distribution between living and post-mortem is 14 and 5. Between children and adults it is 15 and 5. The exact age of the fracture in 14 papers was based on birth injury or detailed clinical records. Note: living patients are many, post-mortem cases few. This may not fully correspond to forensic practice, because in forensic medicine one more often works with the deceased.

t: Quick question: the review and samples
n: Here are three quick questions. First: how many publications were included in the review? Answer: 21 publications, covering the period 1987–2024. Second: which population predominates? Answer: children. Of 21 papers, 15, that is, 71.43%, studied the paediatric group alone. Third: which method was used most often? Answer: plain 2D radiography. Of 21 papers, 15, that is, 71.43%, used only this. The risk of error is here: the most frequently used method, that is, 2D radiography, does not mean the most accurate method. The gold standard is histology.

Now let us see which bones were studied. Most of the samples, 851 of 1289, that is, 66.02%, were from long bones. The most numerous was the radius, 250, that is, 19.39%. From skull bones 158 were studied, that is, 12.26%, and from ribs only 32, that is, 2.48% of samples. Thus injuries of the ribs and long bone metaphyses, which are important for forensic medicine, are little studied; ribs appear in only 4 papers. The clavicle is special: it forms from endochondral and intramembranous ossification, whereas long bones form from endochondral only. Therefore the result is hard to generalise.

Note the distribution of imaging methods. Of 21 papers in total, 15, that is, 71.43%, used plain 2D radiography alone. Radiography together with histology was in 2 papers, one of them with CT. Histology alone in 2 papers, macroscopy in 1 paper, MRI alone in 1 paper. Histology is the gold standard, but is destructive and applicable only after death. One paper added computed tomography, that is, CT; one paper was limited to magnetic resonance imaging, that is, MRI.

t: The chain of radiographic healing stages
n: We move to the chain of radiographic healing stages. The stages from 17 papers on 2D radiography were summarised into 7 overlapping, continuous stages. They come in 5 groups. The first and second stages are swelling and widening of the gap. The third is periosteal reaction, that is, SPNBF, which is the formation of new bone under the periosteum. The fourth is soft, then hard callus. The fifth and sixth are loss of the line and bridging. The seventh is remodelling. Remember: the stages are not strictly sequential; the healing phases overlap considerably.

Frequency of stages and criteria. In radiographic methods the number of stages ranges from 2 to 8, on average 5, with a mode, that is, the most frequent value, of 6. Criteria in the 17 radiographic papers occur as follows: callus formation in 17 papers, periosteal reaction in 13 papers, remodelling in 12 papers, bridging in 10 papers. No two of the six-stage systems assess the same combination of criteria. Attention: the same process is named differently in different papers. That is, terminology is not standardised.

t: Radiographic review: sample size and number of stages
n: In the radiographic review, let us look at sample size and number of stages. The number of patients in 19 papers: 8–162, mean 63.21. Fractures in 13 papers: 9–212, mean 87.54. Images in 11 papers: 31–707, mean 241.91. In 2D radiography, in 17 papers the number of stages ranges from 2 to 8, mean 5, mode 6; only in two tables is a “no healing” stage defined from the beginning. In histology there are more features: Moirangthem 4 stages, 5 days; De Boer 13 features, 1–2+ years; Naqvi 14 features, ≤1 year. With CT, Cappella applied the 13 stages of De Boer; with MRI, Baron identified 9 features in 6 stages and 3 substages.

t: The histological method: the gold standard
n: The histological method is regarded as the gold standard. It shows at the cellular level; radiography cannot show the cascade of cellular events in the first weeks. De Boer gave 13 features, up to 1–2+ years, Naqvi 14 features, ≤1 year, and Moirangthem 4 stages, for the first 5 days. As time since injury increases, histological assessment too becomes variable, imprecise and wide-ranging. Attention: the method is destructive and post-mortem only. It shows only the state of healing at the time of death and is not used in the living.

Here are quick questions. Histology shows the cellular level: the cascade of cellular events not visible on radiographs in the first weeks is revealed only by this method. Histology destroys bone, so it is used only post-mortem. It gives a snapshot of the state of healing at the time of death. Ask yourself: why can histology not be used in a living patient? Which method shows the cellular cascade in the first weeks? There is also a risk of error: SPNBF, that is, new bone formation under the periosteum, is not callus. In the table these are separate stages.

t: Case analysis: several stages in one fracture
n: Now a case analysis: several stages in one fracture. Situation: in abuse, medical care may be delayed. The fracture ends become mobile and the bone continues to be used. As a result the fragments may unite incorrectly or healing may be delayed. Then several healing stages are visible at once in a single injury. Healing stages partly overlap, and the speed differs from person to person. Therefore the age of a fracture is assessed not as one date but as an interval. Question: what error is possible in estimating the age of such a fracture? Why is it dangerous to draw a conclusion from a single stage?

t: Limitations of radiography: clinical and forensic interpretation
n: We consider the limitations of radiography from the standpoint of clinical and forensic interpretation. A clinical radiograph is taken mainly to assess alignment; a cast, however, reduces image detail. At a late stage follow-up is infrequent, because the radiation dose is not justified by clinical benefit. In a fracture without a cast, care may be delayed or obstructed, the schedule with a cast may not match, secondary microtrauma may occur, and the age interval widens. In the Halliday study, of six features only SPNBF was reliably identified between observers.

We compare CT, MRI and micro-CT. MRI has been proposed as a method without radiation; it distinguishes changes of the early, acute phase well, but subtle features are not visible. CT, that is, computed tomography, is more accurate than 2D radiography, as shown in the Cappella study, but if it relies on 2D stages, its accuracy is limited and remains below that of histology. Micro-CT shows bone in 3D without destroying it and reaches detail down to 60 µm, but is used only post-mortem, and the dose is high.

On micro-CT parameters and artificial intelligence. Viero found five histomorphometric parameters in callus: anisotropy, connectivity density, mineral volume, trabecular separation and thickness. These parameters gave a measurable difference with callus age and maturity; after further verification they may provide objective assessment. Sanchez: even on a 2D radiograph, measuring callus thickness gave a more reliable assessment than traditional qualitative features. Artificial intelligence has also been tested, in the studies of Hržić, Kyllonen and Tsai. The Tsai model estimated to within 1 week in 83.7% of cases, but only in infants aged ≤3 months.

t: Influence of observers, age and immobilisation
n: Influence of observers, age and immobilisation. The Tritella AFHS scale worked well with 5 observers; the highest agreement was among radiologists and the anthropologist; agreement rises with broad features, that is, callus present or absent. Infants heal faster; with increasing age the healing time becomes variable, so pooled paediatric tables may not be age-appropriate. With immobilisation, SPNBF and callus are scant and mature lamellar bone appears early; this effect has not been tested, and for ethical reasons cannot be experimentally studied. Artificial intelligence: Hržić distinguished 3 age groups from 7140 radiographs and 3570 fractures; in the Kyllonen trial, manual assessment by the Malone method was more accurate.

t: The problem of standardisation and validation
n: The problem of standardisation and validation. Terminology is not uniform: no two of the most frequently used six-stage systems assessed the same set of features. So far only one paper, Cappella, was conducted with the aim of testing a previously published method, De Boer. Drury and Cunningham compared three methods on 112 long bone fractures in 96 children; some estimates differed by almost 2 months. The direction for the future is clear: to test the methods on fractures of known age and to assess their accuracy, consistency and robustness.

t: Case analysis: when the methods disagree
n: Case analysis: when the methods disagree. Situation: Drury and Cunningham assessed 112 long bone fractures in 96 children by three methods. The true age of the fractures was unknown. Result: no method agreed fully. The length of the time interval and the start and end dates differed, sometimes by almost 2 months. Risk of error: an approximate age is not an exact age. Estimating fracture age is an imprecise method, and caution is needed in a court case. Question: what should one be wary of in the conclusion? Why is it dangerous to write an exact time relying on a single method? Why is it necessary to test methods on fractures of known age?

t: Phases of wound healing: soft tissue
n: Now the phases of wound healing in soft tissue. There are three phases: inflammation, proliferation and maturation. In the inflammatory phase, cells and soluble factors interact. In proliferation, different processes go on in skin and muscle. Skin: re-epithelialisation and new granulation tissue close the wound surface. Muscle: satellite cells multiply, become myocytes and repair the damage. The last phase is maturation, that is, tissue remodelling.

On the study samples. Studies relied mainly on animal and autopsy samples, and sometimes on living people. To take a sample from a living person, permission from a local ethics committee is needed. Note: in an autopsy sample, putrefaction, decomposition, drying and age influence the result. Therefore, in assessing the result, it is necessary to take into account where the sample was taken from.

Morphological analysis and bruise colour. Morphological analysis is the most frequently used method. It is assessed visually, is objective and shows the location of the marker. Estimating age from bruise colour is highly variable, because colour depends on depth, location and skin colour. Haematoxylin-eosin, that is, HE, and Berlin blue show a change 6 hours after injury, but practical application is limited. Immunohistochemistry, that is, IHC, and immunofluorescence, that is, IF, are useful for the early stage. A digital scanner reduces the subjective factor.

Quick questions on soft tissue methods. First question: why is determining the age of an injury from bruise colour considered unreliable? Answer: colour and time of appearance depend on depth, location and skin colour, so they are highly variable. Second question: which method suits early wounds? Answer: a method based on mRNA, that is, messenger RNA, because it changes before protein. There is also a risk of error: extravasation of erythrocytes is regarded as a sign of vitality, but it also appears post-mortem, and therefore is unreliable.

Molecular methods: mRNA, protein and high-throughput analyses. mRNA changes before protein and morphology, so it suits early wounds. Real-time PCR measures mRNA level and is very sensitive. Western blot and ELISA measure the amount of protein and are more sensitive than IHC. A protein microarray shows many proteins in one sample. Gene chips analyse tens to hundreds of genes, are inexpensive and give reproducible results. In PCR, normalisation to a reference gene is essential; some genes change after injury. High-throughput methods reduce cost.

Post-mortem stability and choice of marker. Putrefaction and drying destroy mRNA, that is, messenger RNA, and protein; this is inevitable after death. Therefore, in choosing a marker, substances that remain stable for a certain time after death are preferred. For example, argininosuccinate lyase mRNA is stable for 18 hours, SNAT2 mRNA for 48 hours, and the proteins LC3-II and p62 for 4 days. Cannabinoid receptor-2 mRNA, by contrast, only 3 hours. Attention: stability depends on the marker; between 3 hours and 4 days there is a large difference.

Biomarkers of brain injury. Inflammation after injury to the CNS resembles that of skin and skeletal muscle, but local reactions such as glial cell migration are specific to the CNS. Because neurons are not renewed, brain injury is irreversible. The age of haemorrhage is assessed by haematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemical staining. In diffuse axonal injury, β-amyloid precursor is detected at the site of injury when the axon is disrupted; it is regarded as a sensitive and specific marker. Takamiya, in 2007, showed that the time-dependent expression of 27 cytokines in brain injury may help estimate injury age.

Multi-marker approach and mathematical models. Injury repair is influenced by intrinsic and extrinsic factors, so one parameter is not enough; using several parameters together reduces error. Sun built a model of increase, constancy and decrease from four mRNAs; it narrowed the interval of injury age. Yagi, assessing CD14, CD32B and CD68 together, obtained a more accurate result than with a single marker. Van de Goot and Fronczek developed a probability scoring system. However, no unified system or model for using multiple markers has yet been proposed; the operator's skill also affects the result.

t: Case analysis: a wound in a person with diabetes
n: Case analysis: a wound in a person with diabetes. The situation is a teaching example: the deceased had diabetes mellitus, yet features designed for a healthy person are being applied to determine wound age. In mice, diabetic wound healing differs from ordinary wound healing, so normative wound parameters may not fit it. In peripheral vascular disease wound healing is difficult, and in immunosuppression, that is, weakened immunity, it is delayed. Question: what will the error be if ordinary parameters are applied? Because of delayed healing, the wound age may be misjudged, probably as smaller.

t: Skin IHC/IF review: selection and results
n: Skin IHC and IF review: selection and results. The search was carried out in PubMed and Scopus; IHC is immunohistochemistry, IF is immunofluorescence. The chain is as follows: 326 articles were found, 29 suitable articles remained, 17 more were added from references, and there were 46 articles in total. IHC is easy to use, reliable and can show the location of the required molecules in the tissue. Attention: IHC and IF are not the same; of 46 papers, 32 used IHC alone, 5 IF alone, and 9 both together.

Early markers: coagulation and cytokines. Coagulation markers, for example fibronectin, CD62p and FVIII, are positive at 0–1 hour; the sensitivity of FVIIIra is 100% and specificity 47%. Cytokines: TNFα, that is, tumour necrosis factor, and IL-1β, that is, interleukin-1β, peak at 3 hours, and IL-6 at 12 hours. If IL-1α-positive cells exceed 30%, the wound age is one day or less. Attention: sensitive does not mean specific; for distinguishing antemortem from post-mortem, CD15 and tryptase are more useful.

Immune cells and growth factors. Mast cells peak at 1–3 hours in vital injury; in the post-mortem state they are markedly fewer. TGF-α, that is, transforming growth factor-α, shows an initial response at 10 minutes and a definite response at 30–60 minutes. Other features: CD14 in the Yagi study indicates 1–5 days, more than 50 dendritic cells indicates 4–14 days, and more than 50 % VEGF-positive indicates 7–14 days. Attention: it is not a single feature; the combination of CD14, CD32B and CD68 indicates 1–5 days more precisely.

Enzymes and COX-2 thresholds. If the COX-2-positive fraction, that is, cyclooxygenase-2, exceeds 40%, the injury age may be from 8 hours to 3 days; more than 50% may have forensic significance. If MMP-2-positive cells, that is, matrix metalloproteinase-2, exceed 25, 9–12 days is suggested; if MMP-9-positive cells exceed 30, 3–14 days. Non-specific esterase was found in 40% of samples of vital skin injuries aged 1 hour to 5 days. Attention: the thresholds for COX-2 and MMP-2, 8 hours–3 days and 9–12 days, are not the same; do not mix them up.

Collagen, glycoproteins and basement membrane. α-SMA, that is, smooth muscle actin, positive myofibroblasts appear at about 5 days: the injury is 5 days old or older. Absence of collagens I and VI may indicate that the injury is younger than 6–7 days. Regarding collagens: type III is not detected until 2.5 days, type V is weaker than type III and appears at about 3 days, types I and VI appear consistently at 6–7 days, and type VII, that is, the basement membrane, is seen as fragments at 4 and 8+ days, then with full restoration. Attention: collagen V, 3 days, appears later than collagen III, 2.5 days, and is weaker.

Case analysis: a 5-day-old wound. Situation: at autopsy, α-SMA, that is, smooth muscle actin, positive myofibroblasts were found in a skin wound, collagens I and VI were not detected, and CD14 expression is high. α-SMA-positive myofibroblasts are seen from about day 5. Collagens I and VI usually appear on day 6–7; their absence may mean the wound is younger than 6–7 days. CD14 is highest in wounds of 1–3 days and falls sharply after 3 days. In another study, an increase in the 2–5 day interval was reported. Question: within what interval can the age of this wound lie, and why can one not rely on a single marker?

We compare bone and soft tissue. The stages of bone callus extend from days to years; assessment is carried out with radiography, histology and micro-CT, that is, computed tomography. Skin wound markers change from the first minutes to about 14 days; the main methods are IHC, that is, immunohistochemistry, and mRNA analysis. In both fields, using methods and markers together reduces error; a single indicator is not enough.

Conclusion and rules for remembering. An age estimate is never absolute. In bone, histology is the gold standard, while micro-CT is promising: as a 3D and non-destructive method it complements histology. In estimating wound age, the multi-marker approach is considered the most reliable, but it is more complex and takes more time. Remember: vitality is not wound age. Vitality means that the injury was inflicted during life, whereas wound age shows how much time has passed since then. Also remember: SPNBF is not callus. SPNBF, that is, new bone formation under the periosteum, and callus formation are separate stages.
